**Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984) and Winston Smith**
Orwell's 1949 dystopian novel (Orwell was the pen name of Eric Arthur Blair). It is set in Oceania, ruled by the Party under the ideology Ingsoc (English Socialism) and the all-seeing Big Brother. Winston Smith rewrites history at the Ministry of Truth (Minitrue). He begins an illicit affair with Julia, who outwardly belongs to the Junior Anti-Sex League. The Party's slogans are "War is Peace, Freedom is Slavery, Ignorance is Strength."

**Newspeak and Syme**
The Party's artificial language, built to make dissent unthinkable by shrinking vocabulary. Its words include "doublethink," "thoughtcrime" (crimethink), "unperson," "doubleplusgood," "Miniplenty," and "thinkpol" (Thought Police). The lexicographer Syme works on the eleventh edition of the Newspeak dictionary and is "vaporized" for understanding things too clearly.

**Room 101, O'Brien, and "Do it to Julia!"**
O'Brien, an Inner Party member who pretends to belong to the resistance, betrays Winston and tortures him in the Ministry of Love. Mr. Charrington, the junk-shop owner who rents Winston and Julia a room, turns out to be a Thought Police agent. In Room 101, faced with a cage of rats strapped to his face, Winston breaks and screams, "Do it to Julia!" In prison he meets the poet Ampleforth, jailed for leaving the word "God" in a Kipling poem because there are only twelve rhymes for "rod."

**Emmanuel Goldstein, "the Book," and the Two Minutes Hate**
Goldstein is the Party's arch-enemy, who may not exist, and he is the target of the daily Two Minutes Hate. He is the supposed author of "the Book," The Theory and Practice of Oligarchical Collectivism. The Book describes the endless war among Oceania, Eurasia, and Eastasia over a disputed quadrilateral with corners at Tangier, Brazzaville, Darwin, and Hong Kong.

**Animal Farm: Napoleon and Snowball**
Orwell's 1945 allegorical novella of the Russian Revolution. Inspired by old Major and the song "Beasts of England," the animals of Manor Farm overthrow the farmer Mr. Jones. The pig Napoleon (Stalin) drives out his rival Snowball (Trotsky) and becomes a tyrant. The farm's Hoof and Horn flag is later replaced with a plain green flag.

**Boxer**
The loyal, hardworking cart horse of Animal Farm, whose mottoes are "I will work harder" and "Napoleon is always right." When he collapses, the pigs claim to send him to a veterinarian, but he is actually sold to the knacker (glue maker), and Napoleon uses the money to buy whisky for the pigs.

**"All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others"**
The pigs gradually rewrite the Seven Commandments to justify their privileges, for example forbidding drinking alcohol only "to excess" and sleeping in beds only "with sheets." Finally only this single maxim remains. The novella ends with a card game in which Napoleon and Mr. Pilkington both play an ace of spades, and the animals can no longer tell pigs from men.

**Moses, Mr. Frederick, and Mr. Pilkington**
Moses the tame raven tells the animals about Sugarcandy Mountain, an animal heaven where it is Sunday seven days a week. Animal Farm lies between two neighboring farms: Foxwood, owned by Mr. Pilkington, and Pinchfield, owned by Mr. Frederick, who attacks the farm and blows up the windmill with dynamite.

**"Politics and the English Language"**
Orwell's 1946 essay arguing that vague, bloated prose hides political truth and serves authoritarian regimes. It attacks "dying metaphors," "verbal false limbs," "pretentious diction," and "meaningless words," and it ends with six rules, such as "Never use a long word where a short one will do." It parodies Ecclesiastes ("the race is not to the swift") as "objective considerations of contemporary phenomena compel the conclusion that success or failure in competitive activities exhibits no tendency to be commensurate with innate capacity." It also compares insincerity to a cuttlefish spurting out ink.

**"Shooting an Elephant"**
An essay drawn from Orwell's years as a colonial police officer in Burma. In Moulmein, an elephant in "must" (a frenzied state) kills a coolie. Although the danger has passed, the narrator shoots it in front of a large Burmese crowd "solely to avoid looking a fool." He reflects that "when the white man turns tyrant it is his own freedom that he destroys."

**Other essays**
"A Hanging" describes a condemned Burmese prisoner stepping around a puddle on the way to the gallows. "Why I Write" lists four great motives, including "sheer egoism" and "aesthetic enthusiasm." "Inside the Whale" reviews Henry Miller's Tropic of Cancer through the story of Jonah and attacks W. H. Auden's phrase "the necessary murder." Others include "Decline of the English Murder" (the Cleft Chin Murder versus Jack the Ripper), "The Lion and the Unicorn," an essay calling Kipling a "good bad poet," and his "As I Please" columns for the Tribune.

**Homage to Catalonia and The Road to Wigan Pier**
Homage to Catalonia (1938) recounts Orwell's service in the POUM militia during the Spanish Civil War, alongside commander Georges Kopp, and his disillusionment with the Stalinist communists. The Road to Wigan Pier (1937) is a two-part book: a study of the poverty of the working class in northern England (including the Brooker family's lodging house) and an essay on why socialism was not more popular.

**Burmese Days**
Orwell's first novel, published first in the United States in 1934, about the timber merchant John Flory in colonial Burma. It opens with the corrupt magistrate U Po Kyin plotting to ruin the reputation of Flory's friend Dr. Veraswami.

**Keep the Aspidistra Flying and A Clergyman's Daughter**
In Keep the Aspidistra Flying (1936), the poet Gordon Comstock "declares war" on money and quits his copywriting job at the New Albion advertising agency. He struggles with his unfinished poem London Pleasures, gets help from the publisher Ravelston, and finally settles down and buys an aspidistra, the symbol of middle-class respectability. In A Clergyman's Daughter (1935), Dorothy Hare loses her memory, sleeps rough in Trafalgar Square, and becomes a schoolteacher.
